result.summary: Pausanias explains how Phocis got its name and where it lies. He then recounts the Phocians' wars against the Thessalians, won by buried pots, a desperate resolve, an oracle, and a night attack in white plaster.

scenes.title: Naming and geography of Phocis
scenes.summary: Pausanias tells how Phocis took its name from Phocus and describes its borders and ports.

scenes.title: The buried pots at Hyampolis
scenes.summary: The Phocians bury pots to cripple the Thessalian cavalry, which is lamed and unhorsed.
scenes.stakes: The Phocians risk being overrun by the superior Thessalian cavalry.

scenes.title: Oracle and Phocian Resolution
scenes.summary: The Phocians consult Delphi, lose 300 men under Gelon, and prepare a funeral pile for their families, giving rise to the phrase Phocian Resolution.
scenes.stakes: The Phocians face destruction and the loss of their families and property.

scenes.title: The battle won and statues at Delphi
scenes.summary: Led by Tellias, Rhœus and Daiphantes, the Phocians win; the passwords reveal the oracle's meaning, and statues are dedicated at Delphi.
scenes.stakes: Defeat would mean the death of the Phocians' families and the loss of their land.

scenes.title: The night attack in plaster
scenes.summary: Five hundred Phocians whiten themselves with plaster and terrify the Thessalians in a night attack devised by Tellias.
scenes.stakes: The Phocians risk defeat by the Thessalian camp at the entrance to Phocis.

alias_notes.explanation: The Thessalian watchword names Athene by her Itonian cult title.

notable_quotes.reason: The ambiguous Delphic oracle about mortal and immortal that the battle later explains.
Explains the origin of the Greek phrase Phocian Resolution.

analysis.text: The passage shows cunning and desperation winning against a stronger foe, with an oracle's riddle explained only afterwards.
Pausanias records Phocian traditions from before the Persian invasion, tying them to Delphi's dedications and to a proverbial phrase.

legacy.text: The phrase Phocian Resolution became proverbial among the Greeks for a desperate, all-or-nothing decision.

fun_facts.text: Herodotus also tells of the Phocian pots and the whitened men in his account of the Thessalian wars.

language_notes.text: The Epicnemidian Locrians were a Locrian people living by Mount Cnemis; they held a strip of coast that cut Phocis off from the Lamiac Gulf.
The oracle's riddle speaks of a 'mortal and immortal' fighting together; the Phocians do not understand it until the battle passwords are revealed.
'Phocian Resolution' became a Greek proverb for a desperate, all-or-nothing decision made out of despair.
Itonian Athene was a goddess worshipped by the Thessalians at Itonus. Phocus was a human hero, so the immortal and mortal of the oracle are the two watchwords.
'Plaster' means a white gypsum or lime coating. 'At its full' means the moon was full, making the white figures look eerie and bright.

context_notes.text: The war against Ilium is the Trojan War. The Persian invasion of Greece occurred in 480 BC, so the Thessalian war was earlier.
Seers were prophets who interpreted omens and sacrifices; armies often took them on campaign, and Elis was famed for its seer families.
Delphi, sacred to Apollo, was where Greek cities dedicated statues and offerings to commemorate victories.

literary_notes.text: The Thessalians charge confidently at the ground, and their own cavalry, their great strength, is turned against them by a simple trick.
The enigmatic oracle hints that the battle will bring both mortal and divine victory, and the passwords later explain it.
The funeral pile and orders to kill their own families show the Phocians' grim determination and desperation.
The Thessalians mistake human plaster for a divine apparition, so superstition defeats them.
